subject: Decision: secure ingress for Redwood Private — Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Alex Ramos <alex.ramos@orionai.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com
Cc: Gina Park <gina.park@orionai.com>
Date: Mon, 12 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Redwood Private — connectivity options and constraints

Vanessa,

Thanks for taking this on. We're finalizing architecture for our integration with Redwood Private (on-prem option) and need your guidance on the recommended connectivity pattern. High level constraints:

- Orion's inference clusters live in a managed VPC in us-west-2; we need a secure, auditable path for API calls to customer-managed private deployments behind an AWS VPC.
- We have strict E2E encryption and least-privilege requirements (SOC 2 + healthcare data).
- Expected steady-state qps around 200 rps during peak; occasional bursts up to 800 rps for short windows.
- We want retry/failover behavior to minimize app impact during transient link issues.

Attached is a rough network diagram (orion_network_diagram.pdf) and an initial config suggestion (proposed-mtcp-config.yaml). Questions we care about:
1) Which option gives the best combination of security, predictable latency, and easiest ops at our scale (VPC Peering vs AWS PrivateLink vs Site-to-Site VPN)?
2) Are there any architectural gotchas that would affect multi-AZ routing or cross-account IAM?
3) What would you recommend for a canary/fallback approach during the rollout?

Can we set a 30–45 minute call today or tomorrow to walk this through?

--
Alex Ramos
Sr. Cloud Architect, Orion AI
Alex.Ramos@orionai.com
From: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com
To: Alex Ramos <alex.ramos@orionai.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, marcus_lin@redwood.com, soojin_lee@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 12 Apr 2027 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Redwood Private — connectivity options and constraints

Alex — thanks, this is very clear and the diagram is helpful.

Short answer up front: for Orion's constraints (compliance + bursty qps + multi-AZ predictability) we recommend a primary deployment using AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for production traffic, paired with a Site-to-Site VPN for dev/test and as a low-cost fallback routing path. We do not recommend cross-account VPC Peering as the primary path because it increases blast radius and complicates route table operations across many accounts.

Quick rationale bullets:
- PrivateLink (recommended primary):
  - Pros: preserves IP address isolation, provides stable per-connection ACLs/security groups, supports per-endpoint policy enforcement and private DNS; works well with AWS NLB in front of Redwood Private control plane. Easier to audit for SOC2.
  - Cons: per-AZ ENI/ENI quotas and per-GB interface endpoint data costs at high volumes; you'll want to size endpoints and coordinate with our autoscaling plan.
- Site-to-Site VPN (secondary/fallback):
  - Pros: lower setup friction for dev/staging, good for burst isolation testing, can carry multiple subnets without endpoint proliferation.
  - Cons: higher and variable network latency; MTU and path-MTU issues can impact throughput; not ideal as a sole production path when tight latency SLOs exist.
- VPC Peering (not recommended as primary):
  - Pros: simple L3 connectivity, low per-GB cost.
  - Cons: cross-account peering adds routing complexity, no transitive routing (makes multi-customer hub patterns painful), increased exposure of internal IPs to Redwood — complicates compliance posture.

Canary/fallback suggestion (short):
1) Start with PrivateLink in two AZs for prod canary — route a small % (1–5%) of traffic through the PrivateLink endpoint and monitor 99th percentile latency and error rates.
2) If endpoint capacity or cost is a blocker, route non-critical traffic through the VPN fallback while increasing PrivateLink capacity.
3) Roll forward in increments with AutoRollback on elevated latencies and a pre-agreed throttling window.

I've looped in Karthik and Marcus for deeper network/throughput sizing details and Soojin on platform/ops readiness. Proposed slots: Tue 2027-04-13 10:00 PT or Wed 2027-04-14 09:00 PT — which works for you?

Attachments: proposed agenda (I attached a 1-pager inline to the calendar invite).

Thanks,

--

vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com

From: karthik_iyer@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Redwood Private — connectivity options and constraints

Vanessa / Alex — quick technical notes from my side after scanning the diagram:

On PrivateLink sizing and limits:
- PrivateLink creates ENIs in each AZ for each endpoint; at 200–800 rps you should target NLB + TLS termination at Redwood's side and keep long-lived connections (HTTP/2) to reduce ENI churn.
- Watch ENI and ephemeral port quotas; we recommend configuring connection pooling and keepalive settings on client side.

On VPN fallback behavior and MTU: 
- Site-to-Site VPNs commonly hide PMTU issues; make sure your client path MTU discovery is enabled and test large payloads (chunked embeddings) — we've seen packet fragmentation cause 10–15% tail-latency spikes.

On Peering caveats:
- Cross-account peering requires explicit route table management for each peer. If Orion later needs to connect multiple account VPCs to Redwood, you'll either end up with many peerings or a transit VPC design. Both increase operational overhead.

Operational playbook (short):
1) Create Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) in two AZs, with NLB in front of Redwood Private nodes.
2) Configure health checks and create a small-scale canary target group (5% traffic).
3) Deploy an S2S VPN for dev/staging and configure a BGP route with a higher metric so it is only chosen when PrivateLink is unavailable.
4) Monitor connection count, 99pct latency, and TLS errors for the first 48 hours — auto-scale endpoint capacity if connection saturation observed.

I'll bring throughput numbers and a suggested ENI/endpoint capacity table on the call.

-karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Network Engineer, Redwood Inference

Date: Wed, 14 Apr 2027 16:47:00 -07:00
Subject: Final recommendation and next steps — Orion Private deployment

Alex / Gina — thanks for the call earlier today. Summary + agreed next steps below.

Decision summary (agreed):
- Primary connectivity: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) across 2 AZs. This gives us the most secure, auditable path that aligns with Orion's SOC 2 requirements and preserves IP isolation.
- Secondary/fallback: Site-to-Site VPN (BGP with higher local preference) used for dev/staging and as a failover route only.
- VPC Peering: not used for cross-account production traffic due to routing and compliance concerns; safe to consider only for tightly-coupled partner projects where IP exposure is acceptable.

Action items (owners / ETA):
- Redwood (Karthik): produce ENI/endpoint sizing table and recommended NLB config by Fri 2027-04-16. (attachment: proposed-mtcp-config.yaml)
- Redwood (Marcus): prepare SLO checklist and monitoring hooks (99pct latency, TLS error rate, connection counts) by Mon 2027-04-19.
- Redwood (Vanessa): send SOW draft and pricing estimate for PrivateLink + standby VPN; submit to Orion procurement. (attachment: sow_draft_orion.docx)
- Orion (Alex/Gina): confirm VPC CIDR ranges and any egress inspection appliances by Mon 2027-04-19; share any additional compliance checklist items.
- Legal/Procurement (cross-team): coordinate on contract addendum for network costs and data egress; aim to finalize terms before pilot.

Risks & mitigations: 
- Cost: PrivateLink egress can be material at high volumes. Mitigation: agree on traffic thresholds for autoscaling endpoints and consider tokenization/batching strategies to lower per-GB usage.
- Latency tail: monitor PMTU and large-payload behavior; use HTTP/2 multiplexing and long-lived connections to reduce tail effects.

Attachments included: orion_network_diagram.pdf, proposed-mtcp-config.yaml, sow_draft_orion.docx.

I'll drop the SOW into the HubSpot record (HS-1234) and the shared Drive folder. Alex — if that matches your expectations we'll route to procurement/legal and lock dates for the pilot (target pilot: 2027-05-03).

Thanks everyone — feel free to reply with any redlines.
